title: Recognize compensated shock
stem: After significant fluid loss, a client's blood pressure remains near baseline but pulse rises, extremities cool and urine output falls. What is the best interpretation?
options: Cool hands alone explain the low urine output
The pulse change proves anxiety is the primary problem
Compensation may be maintaining pressure despite reduced perfusion
Shock is excluded until systolic pressure falls below a fixed cutoff
why: Peripheral temperature does not explain the whole pattern of reduced organ perfusion.
Anxiety cannot account safely for the combined clinical trend.
Normal pressure does not exclude evolving shock when other perfusion signs worsen.
Perfusion can deteriorate before marked hypotension develops.
takeaway: Normal pressure does not exclude evolving shock when other perfusion signs worsen.
learningObjective: Recognize reduced tissue perfusion despite a compensated blood pressure.

title: Evaluate response to volume resuscitation
stem: A client receives prescribed fluid resuscitation for hypovolemia. Which changes support improved perfusion? Select all that apply.
options: Urine output increases while peripheral warmth improves
Blood pressure rises while confusion becomes worse
Pulse slows only after a sedative is given
Crackles and oxygen needs increase
Alertness improves toward the client's baseline
why: Renal output and peripheral circulation provide complementary response measures.
One improved pressure reading does not outweigh deteriorating neurological function.
Medication-related rate change does not establish restored perfusion.
These may indicate fluid intolerance rather than successful resuscitation.
Improving mentation suggests better cerebral perfusion.
takeaway: Improving mentation suggests better cerebral perfusion.
learningObjective: Evaluate resuscitation using organ-function and peripheral-circulation trends.

title: Reassess fluids when congestion emerges
stem: A client with heart failure receives a prescribed IV fluid challenge for low pressure. New crackles and increasing breathlessness develop during infusion. What should the nurse do?
options: Pause the infusion and urgently reassess/report the change
Finish the prescribed volume before reassessing breathing
Increase the rate because blood pressure remains low
Ask the client to cough before deciding whether the findings matter
why: Emerging congestion suggests the client may not tolerate continued fluid delivery.
Completing the volume may worsen pulmonary congestion.
Low pressure does not establish that more fluid is safe.
Coughing alone cannot resolve the new fluid-tolerance concern.
takeaway: Emerging congestion suggests the client may not tolerate continued fluid delivery.
learningObjective: Reassess fluid tolerance when pulmonary congestion develops during a prescribed challenge.

title: Recognize possible ischemia without prominent chest pain
stem: An older adult with diabetes develops unexplained sweating, nausea and unusual breathlessness during rest. They deny chest pain. What is appropriate?
options: Ask the client to walk to distinguish anxiety from cardiac symptoms
Prompt assessment for possible acute coronary syndrome
Treat nausea first and reassess only after the next meal
Exclude cardiac disease because discomfort is absent
why: Exertion is inappropriate while acute ischemia is being considered.
Ischemia may present with symptoms other than prominent chest pain.
Delaying cardiac assessment can miss time-sensitive ischemia.
Absence of chest pain does not safely exclude ischemia.
takeaway: Ischemia may present with symptoms other than prominent chest pain.
learningObjective: Consider coronary ischemia when autonomic and respiratory symptoms occur without prominent chest pain.

title: Respond to recurrent symptoms after a nondiagnostic test
stem: A client being assessed for possible coronary ischemia had an initially nondiagnostic ECG. Chest pressure recurs with sweating. What is the best action?
options: Wait for the next routine observation time
Offer an antacid and consider relief diagnostic
Reassess promptly and reactivate the chest-pain pathway
Reassure that the initial ECG ruled out a cardiac cause
why: Recurrent symptoms require reassessment when they occur.
Symptom relief after an antacid cannot reliably exclude ischemia.
An earlier nondiagnostic result does not exclude an evolving event.
Early investigations may not establish the final diagnosis.
takeaway: An earlier nondiagnostic result does not exclude an evolving event.
learningObjective: Reassess recurrent ischemic symptoms despite an initially nondiagnostic ECG.

title: Recognize a changing angina pattern
stem: A client previously had brief exertional discomfort relieved by rest. Pain now occurs at rest and lasts longer. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Continue the same activity plan until the next clinic visit
Increase exercise to improve coronary conditioning
Use the previous stable diagnosis to reassure the client
Urgent assessment of the changed pattern
why: The pattern has changed in a potentially important way.
Exercise during possible instability may worsen ischemia.
An old diagnosis does not establish the safety of new symptoms.
New rest pain or increasing duration can indicate unstable ischemia.
takeaway: New rest pain or increasing duration can indicate unstable ischemia.
learningObjective: Escalate an angina pattern that changes from exertional symptoms to prolonged rest pain.

title: Control bleeding after femoral access
stem: A client recently returned from femoral arterial catheterization has fresh bleeding at the site and a growing hematoma. What should the competent nurse do first?
options: Apply prescribed-protocol direct pressure and summon help
Assist the client to the toilet before reassessing
Cover with another dressing and measure the hematoma later
Remove the dressing and leave the site exposed for observation
why: Immediate local control and escalation address active access-site bleeding.
Movement can worsen bleeding and delay control.
A dressing alone may not control active arterial bleeding.
Observation without bleeding control does not address the immediate threat.
takeaway: Immediate local control and escalation address active access-site bleeding.
learningObjective: Apply immediate protocol-based control for active femoral arterial access-site bleeding.

title: Recognize occult bleeding after arterial access
stem: After femoral catheterization, a client becomes hypotensive with new back/flank pain. The visible groin dressing is dry. What should the nurse suspect?
options: An isolated anxiety response to the procedure
Possible internal bleeding despite a dry external site
Normal soreness from lying flat
A dry dressing excludes procedure-related bleeding
why: Anxiety does not safely explain hypotension and new flank pain.
Retroperitoneal bleeding may occur without obvious dressing saturation.
Hypotension with new pain requires more than comfort measures.
The dressing cannot show blood accumulating internally.
takeaway: Retroperitoneal bleeding may occur without obvious dressing saturation.
learningObjective: Recognize possible internal post-procedure bleeding despite a dry groin dressing.

title: Prioritize symptoms during tachyarrhythmia
stem: A monitor shows a rapid irregular rhythm. The client has new chest pressure, confusion and low blood pressure. What should guide urgency?
options: A previously tolerated rapid pulse makes this episode low risk
The client is awake, so the rhythm can wait for routine review
The evidence of poor perfusion and ischemic symptoms
The rhythm's name must be documented before calling for help
why: Past tolerance does not establish safety during current symptoms.
Wakefulness does not exclude serious hemodynamic instability.
Clinical instability determines the need for immediate escalation and treatment.
Detailed classification must not delay responding to an unstable client.
takeaway: Clinical instability determines the need for immediate escalation and treatment.
learningObjective: Prioritize signs of hemodynamic instability during a rapid irregular rhythm.

title: Assess bradycardia using client condition
stem: A client has a pulse of 38/min, new confusion and faintness. Another client has a usual resting pulse of 52/min without symptoms. Who needs immediate assessment?
options: Both clients have identical urgency based solely on pulse below 60/min
The client at 52/min because symptoms have not developed yet
Neither until a full medication list is obtained
The client at 38/min with altered mentation
why: Clinical baseline and symptoms affect urgency.
The other client already has evidence of compromise.
History must not delay assessment of current instability.
Symptoms indicate impaired perfusion associated with marked bradycardia.
takeaway: Symptoms indicate impaired perfusion associated with marked bradycardia.
learningObjective: Distinguish symptomatic bradycardia from an asymptomatic established low resting pulse.

title: Recognize possible pacemaker capture failure
stem: A client with an implanted pacemaker becomes dizzy. Monitor pacing spikes are repeatedly not followed by the expected ventricular complexes. What is appropriate?
options: Urgently assess perfusion and report possible failure to capture
Assume the visible spikes prove the pacemaker is working
Apply routine reassurance because dizziness is common after meals
Wait for the next device clinic appointment
why: Electrical pacing signals without subsequent depolarization may not produce an effective pulse.
Spikes alone do not demonstrate myocardial capture or perfusion.
The monitor change and symptoms require cardiac assessment.
Potential symptomatic pacing failure requires earlier evaluation.
takeaway: Electrical pacing signals without subsequent depolarization may not produce an effective pulse.
learningObjective: Recognize symptomatic pacing spikes without corresponding ventricular capture.

title: Recognize possible acute aortic disease
stem: A client reports abrupt severe chest pain extending into the back, and arm pressures differ substantially. What is the priority?
options: Use the lower arm reading to classify the client as stable
Activate urgent assessment for a possible acute aortic emergency
Treat it as usual musculoskeletal strain before reassessment
Apply a heat pack and review response before notifying anyone
why: Choosing one pressure does not resolve the unexplained asymmetry.
The abrupt pain and perfusion asymmetry require immediate evaluation.
The combined findings suggest a potentially life-threatening vascular cause.
Comfort measures must not delay time-sensitive assessment.
takeaway: The abrupt pain and perfusion asymmetry require immediate evaluation.
learningObjective: Identify an acute aortic warning pattern from abrupt pain and pressure asymmetry.

title: Escalate suspected aneurysm rupture
stem: A client with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm develops sudden abdominal/back pain, pallor and falling pressure. What should the nurse do?
options: Assist the client to walk to relieve back discomfort
Arrange routine imaging after the next analgesic dose
Activate emergency response and support circulation under protocol
Repeat firm abdominal palpation to confirm the aneurysm
why: Mobilization is unsafe with suspected hemorrhagic instability.
Suspected rupture requires urgent evaluation rather than routine scheduling.
The pattern suggests possible rupture with internal hemorrhage.
Repeated palpation adds no necessary confirmation and delays emergency care.
takeaway: The pattern suggests possible rupture with internal hemorrhage.
learningObjective: Escalate possible aneurysm rupture with circulatory compromise.

title: Identify acute limb ischemia
stem: A client suddenly develops a painful cold pale foot with a newly absent pedal pulse. What is the priority?
options: Apply a compression stocking for suspected venous swelling
Elevate the limb well above heart level
Encourage walking until the foot warms
Urgent vascular assessment while protecting the limb
why: Compression does not treat arterial obstruction and may worsen perfusion.
High elevation can further reduce arterial blood supply.
Exertion increases oxygen demand in an ischemic limb.
Sudden loss of perfusion threatens tissue viability.
takeaway: Sudden loss of perfusion threatens tissue viability.
learningObjective: Recognize and protect a limb with sudden arterial perfusion loss.

title: Recognize progression to ischemic rest pain
stem: A client with peripheral arterial disease previously had pain only when walking. They now wake with foot pain at rest and a cool toe ulcer. What is appropriate?
options: Promptly report worsening limb perfusion
Continue the usual walking plan without review
Apply tight elastic compression to improve circulation
Wait until fever appears to report the ulcer
why: Rest pain and tissue injury suggest more severe ischemia.
A new rest-pain pattern requires reassessment before routine exercise advice.
Arterial insufficiency requires assessment before compression is considered.
Ischemic tissue injury can be serious without infection or fever.
takeaway: Rest pain and tissue injury suggest more severe ischemia.
learningObjective: Report progression from claudication to ischemic rest pain and tissue injury.

title: Track meaningful heart-failure improvement
stem: A client is treated for decompensated heart failure. Which trends support an improving clinical response? Select all that apply.
options: Resting saturation stays unchanged on progressively more oxygen
The client reports less anxiety but cannot finish sentences
Less orthopnea at the same oxygen setting
Daily weight decreases toward the treatment goal with stable perfusion
Edema decreases while dizziness and oliguria develop
why: Increasing support may conceal worsening gas exchange.
Reduced anxiety does not offset severe ongoing breathlessness.
Improved tolerance of reclining suggests less pulmonary congestion.
Weight change is useful when interpreted with circulation and symptoms.
Reduced edema can coexist with harmful intravascular depletion.
takeaway: Improved tolerance of reclining suggests less pulmonary congestion.
learningObjective: Distinguish useful heart-failure decongestion from worsening support or perfusion needs.

title: Identify a heart-failure deterioration report
stem: At home, a client with heart failure needs extra pillows, develops more leg swelling and can walk much less than last week. What is best?
options: Drink extra fluid to improve exercise tolerance
Use bed rest alone until symptoms disappear
Contact the treatment team promptly using the action plan
Wait for the next monthly appointment because edema is chronic
why: Extra intake may worsen congestion without an individualized indication.
Rest does not address possible decompensated heart failure.
The combined changes suggest increasing congestion and declining function.
The change from baseline warrants earlier review.
takeaway: The combined changes suggest increasing congestion and declining function.
learningObjective: Recognize a cluster of worsening home heart-failure symptoms requiring timely review.

title: Recognize possible neurogenic shock
stem: After a high spinal injury, a client is hypotensive with a slow pulse and warm dry skin. What pattern should the nurse report?
options: Blood loss is excluded because the skin is warm
All hypotension after trauma must produce tachycardia
The findings represent uncomplicated sleep
Possible loss of sympathetic vascular tone
why: Other injuries can coexist and still require assessment.
Disrupted sympathetic pathways can alter the expected pulse response.
Hypotension after spinal trauma requires urgent physiological review.
Neurogenic shock can produce vasodilation and relative bradycardia.
takeaway: Neurogenic shock can produce vasodilation and relative bradycardia.
learningObjective: Recognize possible neurogenic shock while continuing assessment for coexisting injuries.

title: Reassess perfusion after a transient pressure response
stem: After initial treatment of shock, blood pressure improves briefly, but urine output remains low and confusion increases. What is the best conclusion?
options: Perfusion may remain inadequate despite the improved reading
The client has recovered because pressure briefly normalized
The low output can be ignored until the next day
Confusion should be treated as agitation before reassessment
why: Organ-function trends show that resuscitation may still be insufficient.
A transient pressure response alone does not demonstrate recovery.
Persistent low output can indicate ongoing renal hypoperfusion.
Sedation may obscure deterioration without correcting its cause.
takeaway: Organ-function trends show that resuscitation may still be insufficient.
learningObjective: Evaluate persistent organ dysfunction despite a transient improvement in blood pressure.

title: Recognize findings of impaired perfusion
stem: A client with an acute circulatory problem is being reassessed. Which findings support impaired organ perfusion? Select all that apply.
options: New confusion compared with baseline
Falling urine output despite a patent catheter
New mottling despite a preserved blood pressure
Warm hands after blankets are applied with unchanged mentation
Usual walking tolerance with unchanged alertness
why: Reduced cerebral perfusion can alter mentation.
Reduced renal perfusion can decrease urine production.
Mottling can signal poor peripheral perfusion even when pressure is maintained.
External warming alone does not establish restored organ perfusion.
Stable function and mentation do not support new organ hypoperfusion.
takeaway: Reduced cerebral perfusion can alter mentation.
learningObjective: Select clinical evidence of impaired cerebral, renal and peripheral perfusion.

title: Maintain hemorrhage control when a dressing saturates
stem: A pressure dressing over an actively bleeding limb wound becomes soaked while help is on the way. What should the nurse do?
options: Remove all pressure whenever the client reports discomfort
Focus on measuring the stain before continuing pressure
Maintain firm pressure and add material as indicated by protocol
Repeatedly lift the dressing to inspect whether clotting occurred
why: Pain needs assessment, but uncontrolled hemorrhage remains an immediate threat.
Measurement should not interrupt active bleeding control.
Ongoing pressure supports hemostasis while definitive help is arranged.
Disrupting the site can disturb developing clots.
takeaway: Ongoing pressure supports hemostasis while definitive help is arranged.
learningObjective: Maintain immediate external hemorrhage control while arranging definitive treatment.

title: Respond to a new suspected deep-vein thrombosis
stem: A postoperative client has new unilateral calf swelling and tenderness without chest symptoms. What is most appropriate?
options: Massage the calf and then repeat circumference
Apply the existing exercise plan without reporting the change
Wait for dyspnea to confirm whether the swelling matters
Arrange prompt assessment and follow the activity plan pending evaluation
why: Massage does not treat possible thrombosis and may be harmful.
A new vascular concern changes the assessment needed before activity.
Potential thrombosis warrants assessment before embolic symptoms develop.
The findings need evaluation for thrombosis before routine mobility decisions.
takeaway: The findings need evaluation for thrombosis before routine mobility decisions.
learningObjective: Escalate suspected venous thrombosis before routine activity decisions.

title: Confirm a concerning pulse deficit
stem: A client reports palpitations. The apical rate is faster than the radial pulse. What should the nurse do next?
options: Assess the rhythm, symptoms and perfusion and report the deficit
Record only the lower rate because it is easier to count
Average the two rates and chart a single normal value
Assume the radial measurement is wrong without rechecking
why: Some contractions may not create a palpable peripheral pulse.
The discrepancy itself is clinically relevant information.
An average obscures the pulse deficit rather than explaining it.
Verification is needed before dismissing a potentially important finding.
takeaway: Some contractions may not create a palpable peripheral pulse.
learningObjective: Verify and report a pulse deficit rather than concealing it in an averaged rate.

title: Recognize ongoing bleeding despite initial hemoglobin
stem: A client with fresh gastrointestinal bleeding is tachycardic and pale. The first hemoglobin result remains within the supplied reference range. What should guide care?
options: Wait for the next day's blood count before reviewing treatment
The active bleeding and circulatory findings require urgent assessment
A normal hemoglobin excludes clinically important hemorrhage
Only the stool colour determines whether escalation is needed
why: Delaying care may allow hemodynamic compromise to worsen.
Early hemoglobin may not yet reflect the full acute blood loss.
Initial concentration can be misleading during acute blood loss.
Circulatory symptoms are critical to judging severity.
takeaway: Early hemoglobin may not yet reflect the full acute blood loss.
learningObjective: Recognize significant acute blood loss despite an initially normal hemoglobin concentration.

title: Assess readiness after a syncopal episode
stem: A client briefly lost consciousness on standing and is now awake. Which assessments help determine whether it is safe to proceed with routine care? Select all that apply.
options: Reassess vital signs, symptoms and return to baseline mentation
Review the event, injury risk and relevant medication changes
Resume unassisted walking because consciousness returned
Treat a normal single supine pressure as a complete assessment
Provide reassurance without checking for injury
why: Recovery should be evaluated rather than inferred from wakefulness alone.
Context can identify ongoing causes or consequences of syncope.
Recurrence and injury risk remain unresolved.
The event may involve posture, rhythm or other factors not captured by one reading.
A fall-related injury can be present despite apparent recovery.
takeaway: Recovery should be evaluated rather than inferred from wakefulness alone.
learningObjective: Assess recovery, injury and ongoing risk after a syncopal episode.
